{"id": "51:52/q11", "question": "What purpose does this recurring pattern serve here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is read as consolation, instruction, warning, or a lesson; these purposes can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q11/p1", "position": "It consoles Muhammad: earlier messengers faced the same denunciation, so he should not grieve.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says believers are omitted for consolation. Iṣlāḥī says the Prophet is neither uniquely opposed nor negligent; al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, Elmālili, and Study Quran stress the parallel."}, {"id": "51:52/q11/p2", "position": "It calls the Prophet to persevere, turn from wrongdoers, and remind receptive hearers.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says God will support him and his companions and that he should continue resolutely despite fabricated stories."}, {"id": "51:52/q11/p3", "position": "It warns Quraysh that rejection may bring the fate of Pharaoh’s followers.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 51:39."}, {"id": "51:52/q11/p4", "position": "Earlier communities’ stories provide lessons for reflective readers.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives this reason for recounting the narratives."}, {"id": "51:52/q11/p5", "position": "It rebukes those who persist in falsehood despite the repeated pattern of accusing messengers of sorcery or madness.", "reasons": "Al-Rummānī and al-Burhān call the recurring accusations the strongest rebuke of persistent adherence to falsehood."}]}
{"id": "51:52/q12", "question": "How does the verse connect with its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "Which neighbouring theme or scriptural parallel is foregrounded.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q12/p1", "position": "The same accusations against Muhammad were made by Meccan unbelievers.", "reasons": "Muqātil is reported by al-Wāḥidī; Study Quran lists sorcery, possession, and other charges."}, {"id": "51:52/q12/p2", "position": "It resumes the opening account of deniers’ discordant speech and their denial of resurrection, before warning of the promised day.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī relates it to 51:8; Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes the closing section’s return to opening themes."}, {"id": "51:52/q12/p3", "position": "It parallels Pharaoh’s denunciation of Moses and other accounts of prophetic rejection.", "reasons": "Study Quran points to 51:39 and to 15:11, 34:34, 36:30, 43:7, and 43:23; it also cites accusations against Muhammad at 10:2, 52:29, 15:6–7, 23:70, 34:8, and 68:51."}]}
{"id": "51:52/q13", "question": "What theological implications are drawn from messengers’ rejection?", "turns_on": "Different theological points attached to the rejection and reception of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q13/p1", "position": "God sends messengers amid widespread ignorance for guidance, while leaving belief uncoerced because forced or desperate belief is unacceptable.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī makes both points."}, {"id": "51:52/q13/p2", "position": "God acts and rules as He wills.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī closes the discussion with this Sunni formulation."}, {"id": "51:52/q13/p3", "position": "What God decrees is good, while evil lies in created things that can both benefit and harm.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this from some people, comparing fire and water, whose inherent forces also harm the poor."}, {"id": "51:52/q13/p4", "position": "Understanding revelation depends on God-given favor and intellect.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī calls the Qur’an a guiding light and cites 39:9, 42:52, 2:26, 22:31, and 4:98; he urges the understanding reader to thank God and the doubter to continue rhetorical study, citing 20:114 and 23:97–98."}]}
{"id": "51:52/q14", "question": "What inward reading is given to the passage?", "turns_on": "The first applies the accusations inwardly; the second expounds nearby monotheistic exhortation.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q14/p1", "position": "Rebellious souls in every age reject outward prophets and inward divine inspirations as magic or madness.", "reasons": "The Taʾwīlāt Najmiyya, quoted by Bursevī, attributes this to satanic refusal, pride, defiance, and transgression fed by comfort and wealth."}, {"id": "51:52/q14/p2", "position": "Monotheism requires fleeing to God and cutting attachment to ego, desire, this world, and the next.", "reasons": "The Taʾwīlāt Najmiyya says the true fugitive finds rest with God and warns of painful distance caused by association, citing 4:48."}]}
{"id": "51:52/q15", "question": "What do the cited grammatical examples say about doubled formulas?", "turns_on": "Whether labbayk is single or dual, alongside examples of repeated action; these excerpts do not discuss a word in 51:52.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q15/p1", "position": "Ḥanānik expresses repeated mercy through a fixed annexed dual-like form and an omitted verb.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares subḥāna Allāh and maʿādh Allāh; al-Khalīl says each blessing continues into another; Ṭarafa’s verse illustrates an appeal; Arab usage has subḥāna Allāhi wa-ḥanānihi and the comparison rayḥānahu."}, {"id": "51:52/q15/p2", "position": "Labbayk and saʿdayk express repeated answering and compliance as fixed accusatives.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares the response 'hearing and obedience'; ḥadhārīk similarly means caution after caution. Arab nominatives samaʿ and ḥanān and accusative samaʿan wa-ṭāʿatan are also reported."}, {"id": "51:52/q15/p3", "position": "Dawālik and ḍarban hādhā dhīka describe reciprocal or successive actions and can be analyzed circumstantially.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās’s line describes one garment torn after another; Sībawayh gives the related phrase and its circumstantial option."}, {"id": "51:52/q15/p4", "position": "Labbayk is a single annexed word like ʿalayk.", "reasons": "Sībawayh reports Yūnus’s analysis."}, {"id": "51:52/q15/p5", "position": "Labbayk is dual like ḥawālayk.", "reasons": "Sībawayh reports al-Khalīl’s evidence from singular ḥanān; some Arabs shorten to lab or ḥawālik, while cited lines resist treating labbayk as a preposition like ʿalayk."}]}
{"id": "51:52/q16", "question": "What do the cited discussions say makes eloquent composition?", "turns_on": "The cited excerpts discuss composition, public challenge, and an unrelated grammatical example; they do not directly gloss 51:52.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q16/p1", "position": "Eloquence lies in authored arrangement of meanings and grammatical choices, not copied word sounds.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī compares naẓm to arranging colors; examples involve ordering, definiteness, ellipsis, pronouns, and repetition. A reciter reproduces sounds without becoming the poet or choosing his syntax."}, {"id": "51:52/q16/p2", "position": "A poem’s luster arises from particular choices of indefiniteness, coordination, comparison, condition, circumstance, order, and tense.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī notes indefinite sawdad and dahr, the understood subject with fa, repeated comparative kāf, balanced conditionals and circumstantial forms ṣārikhan and mustathīban, placement of idh nabā before takūn, choice of takūn over kāna, and wa-ankara ṣāḥib over wa-ankartu ṣāḥiban. He says the opening pleases the listener."}, {"id": "51:52/q16/p3", "position": "The Qur’an has no literary counterpart in preserved earlier Arabic speech, poetry, sermon, letter, or sajʿ.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī argues such a precedent would exist if humans could compose one."}, {"id": "51:52/q16/p4", "position": "The public challenge and widely transmitted failure to meet it suffice to establish the miracle.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports this objection, then answers that the challenge publicly exposes incapacity, removes doubt, and binds eloquent experts through the Qur’an itself."}, {"id": "51:52/q16/p5", "position": "The challenge publicly establishes the proof by making incapacity visible.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī gives this reply to the objection that independent proof would diminish the challenge."}, {"id": "51:52/q16/p6", "position": "In a نعم construction, the specified object of praise or blame can be omitted when context supplies it.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān gives this grammatical example."}]}
{"id": "51:52/q17", "question": "How do the cited discussions explain metaphor?", "turns_on": "Whether metaphor is located in lexical substitution or intended meaning; these examples do not directly gloss ساحر.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q17/p1", "position": "A metaphor such as calling a brave man a lion asserts a lionlike quality; the transfer lies in intended meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says الأسد invokes courage and strength. If it merely replaced شجاع as a synonym, it would gain no eloquence; جعلته أسدا assigns a quality as جعلته أميرا assigns office, and two-object جعل works like صيّر."}, {"id": "51:52/q17/p2", "position": "The account that metaphor simply transfers a word from its lexical meaning is misleading.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī rejects this familiar account with الأسد for brave and بحر for generous."}]}

{"id": "51:53/q01", "question": "What does أَتَوَاصَوْا۟ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:53/q01/p1", "position": "They advised or enjoined one another, passed something along, or appeared to agree on it.", "reasons": "MAJAZ allows mutual agreement or taking a view from one another and says a dominant shared trait can make advice appear to have occurred. WAHIDI-BASIT explains it as mutual instruction to use an accusation; Abu ʿUbayda, reported by IBNJAWZI-ZAD, includes collusion and copying. TABATABAI defines mutual enjoining as a people's advising one another."}]}
{"id": "51:53/q02", "question": "What does بِهِۦ refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun points to the repeated charge, rejection of the message, or belief in it.", "positions": [{"id": "51:53/q02/p1", "position": "The repeated accusation that the messengers, especially Muhammad, were sorcerers or madmen.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL identifies the charges against Muhammad as poet, sorcerer, and madman and the older peoples' charges against their messengers as sorcerer or madman. NASAFI-FULL, TABATABAI, and the rhetorical readings identify the pronoun with the accusation; STUDYQURAN specifies calling the Prophet a sorcerer or possessed."}, {"id": "51:53/q02/p2", "position": "Denial of the messenger, truth, or revelation.", "reasons": "Qatāda says predecessors instructed successors to lie, deny the truth, or deny the messenger, as reported by ABDURRAZZAQ, TAB-FULL, and WAHIDI-BASIT. Muqātil, reported by WAHIDI-BASIT, says to speak this way about their messenger. STUDYQURAN reports that the urging entails denial of God and revelation."}, {"id": "51:53/q02/p3", "position": "Belief, which they do not exhort one another to embrace.", "reasons": "STUDYQURAN reports this alternative reading from Āl together with a negative understanding of the question."}]}
{"id": "51:53/q03", "question": "What force does the question أَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِهِۦ have?", "turns_on": "Whether the interrogation chiefly voices rebuking wonder or directly negates the proposed exhortation.", "positions": [{"id": "51:53/q03/p1", "position": "It reproaches or expresses astonishment at the same charge appearing among separated generations, as though they had instructed one another.", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ and al-Zajjāj as reported by WAHIDI-BASIT call the opening hamza both interrogative and rebuking. BAGHAWI-FULL calls its alif reproachful; QURTUBI-FULL adds astonishment. IBNATIYYA-FULL, RAZI-FULL, ALUSI-FULL, and KURANYOLU-TEFSIR stress wonder at distant generations converging. STUDYQURAN reports wonder that people would urge denial of God and revelation; ISLAHI likens it to passing down a will. RUMMANI calls the recurrence of the accusation across generations the strongest rebuke for persistence in falsehood; BURHAN likewise calls the verse the strongest rebuke of persistent adherence to falsehood."}, {"id": "51:53/q03/p2", "position": "It denies that such mutual exhortation took place.", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL reports this as an alternative force of the question. STUDYQURAN reports Āl's negative reading, in which the pronoun instead means belief."}]}
{"id": "51:53/q04", "question": "Why did generations repeat the same denunciation?", "turns_on": "Whether similar accusations require transmission or arise independently from the same transgressive character; distance between generations is repeatedly cited against direct counsel.", "positions": [{"id": "51:53/q04/p1", "position": "Their shared transgression produced the same denial independently, without actual counsel across generations.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL, NAHHAS, WAHIDI-BASIT, IBNATIYYA-FULL, TABRISI, RAZI-FULL, QURTUBI-FULL, BAYDAWI-FULL, NASAFI-FULL, ABUHAYYAN-FULL, BIQAI-FULL, BURSEVI, ALUSI-FULL, ELMALILI, ISLAHI, and KURANYOLU-TEFSIR attribute recurrence to rebellion, not coordination; several note that the generations were too far apart or never met. Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by WAHIDI-BASIT and BAGHAWI-FULL, says prosperity bred rebellion and denial; RAZI-FULL adds self-sufficiency and forgetfulness of God and compares wealthy subjects who later resist a king's summons. IBNKATHIR-FULL says later hearts resembled earlier hearts. BIQAI-FULL reports Ibn al-Zubayr's emphasis on arrogance and darkened hearts, alongside 32:13 and God's ability to guide every soul. BURSEVI calls the disposition innate; KURANYOLU-TEFSIR adds prejudice and stubbornness."}, {"id": "51:53/q04/p2", "position": "Earlier generations actually instructed later ones to deny the messenger or repeat the accusation.", "reasons": "Qatāda's reports in ABDURRAZZAQ, TAB-FULL, and WAHIDI-BASIT describe predecessors instructing successors to lie or deny. Muqātil, reported by WAHIDI-BASIT, says they instructed later people what to say about their messenger. ZAJJAJ says the first advised the last. WAHIDI-WAJIZ takes the rebuke as implying that some instructed others; KURANYOLU-TEFSIR reports Tabarī's formulation as intergenerational transmission."}, {"id": "51:53/q04/p3", "position": "The charge persisted as inherited thinking or a cultural pattern.", "reasons": "ASAD-NOTES frames it as inherited thinking while also explaining rejection through arrogance. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR explicitly raises cultural inheritance but rejects it as the explanation."}]}
{"id": "51:53/q05", "question": "Who are the rebellious people?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate pronoun is taken specifically for Quraysh or the recurrent class of opponents.", "positions": [{"id": "51:53/q05/p1", "position": "The Meccans or Quraysh who rejected Muhammad.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL names Quraysh as recipients of the rhetorical challenge. IBNJAWZI-ZAD explicitly identifies the addressed people as Meccans. ISLAHI compares Quraysh with earlier rejecters."}, {"id": "51:53/q05/p2", "position": "Rejecters of messengers across earlier and later generations.", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, TABRISI, RAZI-FULL, QURTUBI-FULL, BAYDAWI-FULL, and others compare people of separated eras. TAB-FULL names Noah's people, ʿĀd, Thamud, and Pharaoh's people alongside Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "51:53/q06", "question": "What does طَاغُونَ describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:53/q06/p1", "position": "People who exceed bounds through arrogance, corruption, disobedience, and denial.", "reasons": "NAHHAS says they overstep God's commands and prohibitions; WAHIDI-BASIT says they exceed bounds in disobedience. IBNATIYYA-FULL describes earthly arrogance, corruption, and defiance; BIQAI-FULL adds excess in unbelief and wrongdoing and sees transgression as ingrained in the pronoun's subjects, whom God ruins through complete power and knowledge. Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by WAHIDI-BASIT and BAGHAWI-FULL, links rebellion to divine gifts and abundance. ASAD-NOTES calls it overweening arrogance."}]}

{"id": "51:53/q13", "question": "What is sound and what produces it?", "turns_on": "Whether sound is the heard quality itself, a body, or the physical event that causes it; Rāzī repeatedly distinguishes audible sound from visible processes.", "positions": [{"id": "51:53/q13/p1", "position": "Sound is heard directly; air undulation, generated by impact or forceful separation, is its cause.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL distinguishes sound's heard essence from its cause, rejecting visible processes as definitions because sound itself is invisible. He says undulation unfolds through successive impacts and pauses rather than one movement between fixed endpoints; impact is forceful contact and tearing is forceful separation. He refers readers to his rational works for the phoneme."}, {"id": "51:53/q13/p2", "position": "Sound is a quality arising from compressed, undulating air between an impacting and an impacted body.", "reasons": "Avicenna, as reported by RAZI-FULL, gives this account; Rāzī replies that it describes sound's cause if accepted, rather than its essence."}, {"id": "51:53/q13/p3", "position": "Sound itself is a body.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL reports this attribution to al-Naẓẓām but doubts he held it: bodies share corporeality but not sound, are visible and tangible while sound is not, and persist while sound does not. Rāzī suggests al-Naẓẓām may instead have meant that air undulation causes sound."}, {"id": "51:53/q13/p4", "position": "Sound is the collision of solid bodies.", "reasons": "Some, reported by RAZI-FULL, define it this way. Rāzī objects that collision is visible contact whereas sound is not visible."}, {"id": "51:53/q13/p5", "position": "Sound is impact, tearing apart, or motion's undulation.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL reports and rejects these definitions because the proposed states are visible but sound is not."}]}

No specific application to this verse is supplied."}]}

{"id": "55:7/q01", "question": "How is السماء read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether السماء is an object governed by an implicit verb or a nominal subject, and which earlier clause supplies the syntactic parallel.", "positions": [{"id": "55:7/q01/p1", "position": "It is accusative, governed by an understood verb explained by رفعها.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas calls this coordination with a like implied verb. Ibn Jinni, Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, and Abu Ali attach it to the nearby يسجدان clause; al-Alusi finds attachment to the larger nominal clause mismatched, while other grammarians allow that contrast and al-Tibi relates it to the sun and moon clause. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Samin, and al-Alusi identify an elided governor; al-Samin calls it ishtighal and cites 36:39 and Sibawayh's allowance without a resumptive pronoun, against al-Akhfash's requirement. Al-Farra says almost all read without such a pronoun. Ibn Jinni argues against Abu al-Hasan's ban on coordination of unlike case positions: an unspoken case position has no force, as omitted pronouns and this accusative reading show. Al-Burhan gives this as a case of an omitted governor explained by an expressed verb and as verbal matching after the trees' prostration, comparing 5:6. Elmalılı says the fronted object is resumed by a pronoun."}, {"id": "55:7/q01/p2", "position": "It is nominative as the subject of a full nominal clause coordinated with a preceding nominal clause.", "reasons": "Abu al-Sammal transmits this noncanonical reading. Ibn Jinni prefers it because the whole nominal sentence matches والنجم والشجر يسجدان; al-Tabrisi reports his preference. Al-Razi relates it to the opening nominal sentence. Al-Alusi relates it to 55:6. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also note the reading."}]}
{"id": "55:7/q02", "question": "What does God's raising of the sky mean?", "turns_on": "Whether raising describes physical location, exalted rank, celestial order, or an inward ascent; several authors allow more than one sense.", "positions": [{"id": "55:7/q02/p1", "position": "God created the sky physically elevated above earth, supporting or holding it aloft.", "reasons": "Muqatil and those reported by al-Wahidi and al-Bursevi specify five hundred years' distance; al-Wahidi and al-Zajjaj say God prevents its fall. Al-Bursevi reports its formation from smoke above earth's water and roof function. Al-Alusi says it was high from creation, not first low and then lifted. Ibn Ashur says raising entails creation and means making it high without pillars, like a tailor making a pocket wide. Al-Tabataba'i says either the upper direction was made high or celestial bodies were positioned above earth after separation (21:30). Elmalılı calls heaven the encompassing cosmos; Kur'an Yolu calls it cosmic space with galaxies and ordered bodies. Islahi cites 31:10 and 67:3–4 for the columnless, faultless sky and describes invisible gravitational columns. Elmalılı's Turkish rendering calls the heaven beautiful."}, {"id": "55:7/q02/p2", "position": "Its elevation also signifies rank: the sky is the source of divine decrees and commands and abode of revelatory angels.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Baydawi, and al-Bursevi associate its height and firmness with God's majesty and sovereignty. Al-Tabataba'i allows spiritual elevation if angelic stations and sources of revelation are included; Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu likewise allow a spiritual sense."}, {"id": "55:7/q02/p3", "position": "The sky is an ordered celestial realm with fixed stars, horizons, seasons and measured rain.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri adds protection from disorder. Islahi describes a faultless balanced sky and its invisible gravitational supports; Kur'an Yolu describes galaxies and bodies moving in order."}, {"id": "55:7/q02/p4", "position": "In an inward reading, the sky is intellect raised toward spirit and heart.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani pairs this with justice lowered to self and body and with the order of human virtues."}]}

{"id": "55:7/q04", "question": "What is the balance God set?", "turns_on": "Whether mizan names the virtue of justice, a concrete weighing device, a wider standard, revealed guidance, judgment, cosmic equilibrium, or an inward or eschatological measure. Ibn Atiyya calls the familiar scale one instance of the broader metaphor. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur, and others compare scripture and balance in 57:25. Al-Baydawi, al-Bursevi, and al-Alusi stress each recipient's due and each right fulfilled; al-Biqa'i says this orders both cosmic realms. Al-Alusi prefers this sense for its breadth despite the following command's fit with physical scales. Ibn Ashur says mizan is literally an instrument but metaphorically justice; he and the Study Quran note justice across creation and exchange."}, {"id": "55:7/q04/p2", "position": "It is a physical instrument, or class of instruments, for weighing and measuring fairly.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Dahhak repeatedly hold this view; al-Baghawi says its basic sense is measurement. Al-Kashifi gives established scales as one interpretation of وضع. {"id": "55:7/q11", "question": "What does the concrete imagery of weighing illustrate about figurative expression?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:7/q11/p1", "position": "A concrete image can convey an associated quality or effect through its characteristic use and context.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani's staff examples show that a weak staff may suggest a gentle shepherd while a firm one suggests effective herd control; both can indicate good care by different routes. {"id": "55:9/q01", "question": "What does it mean to establish the weight?", "turns_on": "Whether establishing weight specifies leveling a physical scale, sustaining that practice, or extending the measure of justice to conduct and the inward life.", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q01/p1", "position": "Set the scale straight and weigh fairly in giving and receiving.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies the scale's tongue; Abu al-Darda, Ata, Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Muqatil specify a level tongue or beam (Thalabi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Qurtubi, Alusi).
